title: Seneca's last hours
hookLine: ordered to die by Nero, he tells his friends he leaves them the one thing he has, the image of his life

cards: A soldier arrives at a country house with the emperor's order: the man inside is to die. The man is Seneca.

He came home from exile to tutor a boy named Nero; the boy became emperor, and for a few years Seneca helped steer the empire. Then Nero changed. Seneca tried to step away, even offering to hand back his fortune.
Then a plot to kill Nero was uncovered. Whether Seneca was part of it, nobody knows. Nero didn't need to know.

teach.b: The Roman historian Tacitus, writing some decades later, tells it plainly. Seneca, calm, asks for his will so he can leave gifts to his friends. The soldier refuses.
So he turns to the friends around his table.

teach.h: THE ONLY THING HE STILL HAS.
teach.b: Since he can't thank them as they deserve, he'll leave them the only thing he still has, and the most beautiful: the image of his life. Remember it, and they'll be known for good character and faithful friendship.
Seneca, gently and then more firmly, asks where their philosophy has gone, all those years of preparing for exactly this.

His wife, Paulina, is with him and wants to die with him. Tacitus says Nero, not wanting to seem too cruel, ordered her kept alive; she lived on some years, pale for the rest of her life, remembering him.
Seneca died, as ordered. This isn't told to make death look noble. It's told for one line.
The money, the house, the will: all of it could be taken. What was left was the image of how he'd lived. Not a statue, not even his writings: the picture of a life his friends would carry.
And a question for any of us, long before the end.
If the people who love you described the image of your life in one line, what would it be? Is it the line you'd choose?

how: Some people reflect on the legacy of character they hope to leave, sometimes by writing a short statement of how they want to be remembered and returning to it as a guide.

a Roman will that leaves gifts to friends

games.q: you're Seneca. the soldier has refused you your will, and your friends are around the table. what do you leave them?
o: nothing. there's nothing left to leave.
games.why: the only thing he still had, and the most beautiful: the image of his life. if they remember it, they'll be known for good character and faithful friendship.

practice: This one is about living. Sit, let the breath settle, and picture the people who love you around a table, remembering how you were, not what you achieved: kind, funny, always showed up.
Let a phrase come, then ask whether it's the image you'd choose, and what you'd add.

wordCard.voice: imago vitae, Latin for the image of a life, which is what Seneca left his friends when he was ordered to die.

orig.note: Latin: the image of a life. Tacitus reports Seneca leaving his friends imaginem vitae suae, the image of his life.

carryVoice: Your line: the image of a life. Yours is still being made, one ordinary day at a time. That's day thirty-three.

sources.ref: Tacitus, Annals 14.53–56 (Seneca offers to return his wealth)
